deep.reconstruction:
Context (previous page): Gauss states a theorem for Listing ('Zur Ansicht für H. Listing'). For real A,B,C,a,b,c put p=A+B+C, q=AB+AC+BC-a^2-b^2-c^2, r=ABC+2abc-Aa^2-Bb^2-Cc^2. Then the cubic X=x^3-p x^2+q x-r has three real roots. In modern terms p, q and r are the trace, the sum of the principal 2x2 minors, and the determinant of the real symmetric matrix M=[[A,c,b],[c,B,a],[b,a,C]]. X is its characteristic polynomial, so the theorem says a real symmetric 3x3 matrix has real eigenvalues. Cases I-III (some of a,b,c zero) were settled on the previous page by factoring or by sign changes.

This page, case IV (a,b,c all nonzero). Gauss reduces to a case with c=0, using complex numbers instead of angles.

Step 1. Define real g,h by sqrt(A-B+2ci)=g+hi, citing Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum art. 32 for the square root of a complex number. Squaring gives:
(1) A-B=g^2-h^2
(2) c=gh

Step 2. Set A'=A+h^2 and B'=B-h^2. Then:
(3) A'-B'=A-B+2h^2=g^2+h^2
(4) A'+B'=A+B
(5) A'B'=AB+h^2(B-A)-h^4=AB-h^2(g^2-h^2)-h^4=AB-g^2h^2=AB-c^2 (the intermediate steps are mine).
So A' and B' are the eigenvalues of the 2x2 block [[A,c],[c,B]]. Note that A'-B'=|A-B+2ci|=sqrt((A-B)^2+4c^2).

Step 3. Substituting (4) and (5) into p, q, r:
(6) p=A'+B'+C
(7) q=A'B'+(A'+B')C-a^2-b^2. The manuscript writes A'C'+B'C', where C' must mean C.
(8) r=A'B'C+2abc-Aa^2-Bb^2, since C(AB-c^2)=A'B'C.

Step 4. Define real a',b' by a'+b'i=(a+bi)(g+hi)/sqrt(g^2+h^2). The factor (g+hi)/|g+hi|=e^{i theta} has unit modulus, with tan 2theta=2c/(A-B). Hence conjugation gives a'-b'i=(a-bi)(g-hi)/sqrt(g^2+h^2), and multiplying the two gives:
(9) a^2+b^2=a'^2+b'^2

Continuation (next page).
- Squaring and taking real parts: ((a^2-b^2)(g^2-h^2)-4abgh)/(g^2+h^2)=a'^2-b'^2.
- With (1)-(3) this becomes (a^2-b^2)(A-B)-4abc=(a'^2-b'^2)(A'-B').
- Adding (a^2+b^2)(A+B)=(a'^2+b'^2)(A'+B') gives Aa^2+Bb^2-2abc=A'a'^2+B'b'^2.
- Hence r=A'B'C-A'a'^2-B'b'^2 and q=A'B'+A'C+B'C-a'^2-b'^2.
So p, q, r are unchanged when (A,B,C,a,b,c) is replaced by (A',B',C,a',b',0), and case IV reduces to cases I-III.

Modern reading: this is an orthogonal similarity by a plane rotation in the (1,2)-coordinate plane through angle theta, chosen to annihilate the (1,2) entry. That is exactly one Jacobi rotation, i.e. the principal-axis rotation of the binary form Ax^2+2cxy+By^2. Complex multiplication encodes the rotation of the vector (a,b) of off-diagonal entries in the third row and column.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page. All of (1)-(9) check out symbolically.
Notational slip in (7): the manuscript has A'C'+B'C', but C is not transformed, so this should read A'C+B'C. The same slip recurs in (10) on the next page.
Minor bookkeeping: the label (9) is used twice, for aa+bb=a'a'+b'b' here and for the new r on the next page. The equation numbers (6)-(8) and (9) appear to be written over.
Implicit (justified) assumption: g^2+h^2≠0. This holds because c≠0 in case IV.

results.what: Reality of the roots of the characteristic cubic of a real symmetric 3x3 matrix (secular equation), with p, q, r written explicitly as trace, sum of principal minors, and determinant
results.modern_name: Real eigenvalues of real symmetric matrices (3x3 case of the spectral theorem)
results.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1773, principal axes) and Laplace (1776, secular equation) for special cases; Cauchy (1829) for general n; later proofs by Sturm, Jacobi, Kummer (1843), Sylvester

results.what: Reduction of the case a,b,c≠0 to c=0 by a plane rotation chosen via sqrt(A-B+2ci)=g+hi, so that tan 2θ=2c/(A-B), preserving trace, principal-minor sum and determinant
results.modern_name: Jacobi (Givens) rotation / principal-axis rotation eliminating an off-diagonal entry, encoded by complex multiplication
results.usually_credited_to: Euler/Lagrange for removing the xy term of a conic; Jacobi (1846) for the iterative eigenvalue method

results.what: Invariance identities A'+B'=A+B, A'B'=AB-c^2, a'^2+b'^2=a^2+b^2, A'a'^2+B'b'^2=Aa^2+Bb^2-2abc
results.modern_name: Orthogonal invariance of the trace, principal minors and determinant under the rotation

deep.surprise_reason: The theorem was well known by Gauss's late period (Lagrange, Laplace, Cauchy 1829). The single rotation eliminating one off-diagonal term is the classical principal-axis transformation of a binary quadratic form. The elegant complex-number encoding and the Jacobi-rotation flavour are a nice unpublished didactic detail, written for Listing, but not a priority claim.
